summary:
İstanbul stands under the national framework in force across Turkey, where hostility toward LGBTI+ people has been formalised as state policy. Kaos GL's 2025 annual report, "The Year of the Family: A Major Siege Against LGBTI+ People", records that pattern operating in İstanbul directly, including intensified practices of sealing or closing the homes of LGBTI+ residents that obstruct access to housing.

The same monitoring counts six violations of the right to life across Turkey in 2025, three of them recorded as hate-motivated, with trans people the group most affected. Torture and ill-treatment violations nearly doubled, rising to 89 from 51. One LGBTI+ association was closed and criminal cases were opened against 11 of its members. The state keeps no official hate-crime statistics, so these figures rest on civil-society monitoring rather than on government record-keeping.

Street-level policing in İstanbul targets trans women specifically. On 31 July 2025 police in the Beyoğlu district stopped around 20 trans women for identity checks, recorded their names and filmed video of the encounters; those stopped described the operation as profiling. Foreign visitors stopped at such checkpoints must produce original identity documents, which makes every check an occasion on which a passport gender marker can be compared against presentation.

Public assembly is closed to LGBTI+ people in the city. The Governorship of İstanbul has denied permission for and locally banned pride parades on security and public-order grounds since 2015, with the 2016 to 2018 bans stated explicitly. Police used water cannon against the march on 29 June 2015. Suppression escalated thereafter: blockades and tear gas in 2021 with 25 arrested; 373 arrested in 2022; 113 arrested in 2023; and 11 arrests in 2024, three of them minors.

The 2022 operation is documented in detail. On 26 June 2022 riot police dispersed the march at Taksim Square, blockaded streets in the nearby Cihangir neighbourhood and shut down public transport to the square, detaining 373 people including AFP photojournalist Bülent Kılıç, who were released after a night in custody according to Kaos GL. The district governor's offices of Kadıköy and Beyoğlu had banned all LGBTI+ Pride Week events for seven days beforehand, and eight further people were detained at a Pride march in İzmir.

Organisers' adaptations have not reopened the space. In 2024 İstanbul Pride was moved to non-Taksim public spaces and organisers issued fake meeting calls to thwart police, after which 11 people were arrested, three of them minors. The scale of what is now prohibited is established by the 2014 march, which drew more than 100,000 participants and remains the largest LGBT event in Turkey's history.
tangentialFactors:
The İstanbul figures sit inside a national pattern of detention. Kaos GL's national monitoring for 2025 recorded 299 detention decisions, and the roundup of around 20 trans women in Beyoğlu is one instance of the identity-check practice applied across the country, including at transit checkpoints in holiday destinations where fines of up to 3,000 Turkish lira apply to foreigners who cannot produce original photo identification.

Detention at Pride is not confined to İstanbul. Eight people were detained at a Pride march in İzmir on the same 2022 weekend, indicating that the İstanbul bans form part of a country-wide approach to Pride events rather than a municipal exception.

Recorded deaths differ by source and method. Kaos GL counts six violations of the right to life in 2025 with three classified as hate-motivated, while other reporting for the same year links six deaths to anti-LGBTQ violence with three classified as hate killings; the alignment of the totals suggests a shared underlying count, but the categories used by each are not stated identically.

The absence of official hate-crime statistics in Turkey leaves the assessment dependent on civil-society monitoring. Kaos GL's report, the Truth Justice Memory Center's Pride monitoring and NGO coordination through Human Rights Association branches are the working evidence base, which means figures can be contested by authorities in a way that state-recorded data would not be.

Comparatively, the trajectory runs against the direction taken in several European jurisdictions. The 2014 İstanbul march drew over 100,000 participants, at the time the largest LGBT event in Turkey's history, and the subsequent decade of bans, water cannon, tear gas and mass arrest marks a sustained contraction of assembly rights rather than isolated incidents.
localsOnly:
Housing is a live site of enforcement for LGBTI+ residents of İstanbul. Kaos GL's 2025 monitoring records intensified practices of sealing or closing homes in the city, obstructing access to housing; the district governor's office ordered trans women's apartments on Bayram Street sealed in March 2024, and residential blockades with drones and raids followed in July 2025.

Organised LGBTI+ activity carries criminal exposure. One LGBTI+ association was closed during 2025 and criminal cases were opened against 11 of its members, while torture and ill-treatment violations recorded nationally rose to 89 from 51 the previous year.

Residents have no official hate-crime statistics to rely on. The state keeps no such record, so protection claims, sentencing arguments and policy monitoring depend on civil-society documentation produced by Kaos GL and coordinated human-rights groups.

Assembly remains prohibited in practice. The Governorship of İstanbul has refused permission for pride parades every year since 2015, and in 2022 the Kadıköy and Beyoğlu district governor's offices banned all Pride Week events for seven days, with arrests following in 2023 and 2024 including of minors.
outOfScopeNotes:
Unresolved: whether the draft legislative package reported before the Turkish government as of October 2025, which would effectively criminalise LGBTI+ people, has since been passed is not established in the sources cited here. Reporting indicates it had not been passed when last covered, while authorities were already applying its prohibitions in practice.

Unresolved: the arrest totals for İstanbul Pride in 2021, 2022, 2023 and 2024 are drawn from a Wikipedia article and from Duvar English citing Kaos GL; the underlying police or prosecutor records are not independently sourced in this inventory, and figures for 2022 appear in two sources with the same total.

Unresolved: whether the sealing and closing of LGBTI+ residents' homes in İstanbul continued after the 2025 monitoring period, and whether any of the sealing orders were challenged in court, is not documented in the available material.

Unresolved: the relationship between the six right-to-life violations counted by Kaos GL for 2025 and the six deaths linked to anti-LGBTQ violence reported elsewhere for the same year is not reconciled in the sources; whether these are the same incidents counted under different criteria is not stated.

Not sourced here: whether any legal challenge to the İstanbul Governorship's standing refusal of pride permits has been brought before Turkish administrative courts, and the current status of the criminal cases opened against the 11 members of the closed LGBTI+ association.
